Vocabulary
Brain Teaser: What Do You Know About the Brain and Decision Making?
analyze
to examine something in detail in order to understand it or explain it
consequence
a result or effect of an action or decision
dilemma
a situation where you have to choose between two difficult options
evaluate
to judge or calculate the quality, importance, or value of something
impulse
a sudden, strong desire to do something without thinking about it
instinct
a natural, inborn behavior or reaction that you do without thinking
logic
reasoning that uses clear, sensible thinking based on facts
outcome
the result or effect of an action, meeting, or process
peer pressure
the influence that people of the same age or social group have on each other
predict
to say what you think will happen in the future based on current information
risk
the possibility of something bad happening; a dangerous situation
weigh
to consider the good and bad aspects of something before making a decision
bias
a tendency to prefer one person, thing, or idea over another in an unfair way
rational
based on clear thought and reason rather than emotions

Grammar
The Conditional
First Conditional — Real Possibilities
Use for real or likely situations in the future.

If + present simple, will + base verb
If I study hard, I will pass the exam.
If it rains tomorrow, we will stay home.
Will you call me if you need help?
Second Conditional — Hypothetical Situations
Use for unreal, imaginary, or unlikely situations in the present or future.

If + past simple, would + base verb
If I had more money, I would buy a new car.
If she lived closer, we would see each other more often.
Would you travel the world if you won the lottery?
Key Differences
First Conditional: The situation is real and possible. The speaker believes it could happen.
If I eat too much sugar, I will feel sick. (This happens to me regularly.)
Second Conditional: The situation is imaginary or unlikely. The speaker does not believe it will happen.
If I ate too much sugar, I would feel sick. (But I never eat too much sugar.)
Other Words Instead of "If"
Unless = if not
As long as = only if
Provided that = on the condition that
I will not go unless you come with me.
As long as you finish your homework, you can go out.
You can borrow my car provided that you drive carefully.
Important: In the second conditional, use were for all subjects after "if" in formal English.

✅ If I were you, I would apologize. (formal)
✅ If I was you, I would apologize. (informal, also acceptable)
Pronunciation: Thought Groups in Conditional Sentences

When speaking, pause slightly after the if-clause and before the main clause. This helps the listener understand the two parts of the sentence.

"If I study hard // I will pass the exam."
"If I had more money // I would buy a new car."

Three Everyday Decisions
Exercise A — Before you listen: Discuss

Think of three everyday decisions you make: what to eat, what to wear, whether to study or relax. What factors influence your choices? Are they logical or emotional?

Exercise B — Listen and complete the decisions

Three people describe a decision they made today. Complete the missing information.

Decision 1 — What to eat for lunch

"I was really craving a burger, but I (decide) to get a salad instead. If I (eat) the burger, I (feel) sluggish all afternoon. The salad gave me more energy, and I (be able) to focus better in my afternoon classes."

Decision 2 — Whether to go to the gym

"It was raining, and I almost stayed home. But I thought, if I (skip) the gym today, I (probably skip) tomorrow too. So I went. It was hard at first, but after ten minutes I felt great. Sometimes the hardest part is just starting."

Decision 3 — Helping a friend

"My friend asked to copy my homework. I (be) in a real dilemma. If I (say) yes, I (help) him in the short term, but he (not learn) anything. In the end, I offered to explain the problems instead. It took longer, but it was the right thing to do."

Reading
The Teenage Brain: Why Teenagers Act the Way They Do

🧠 The Teenage Brain

Why do teenagers take risks? Why do they sometimes seem to ignore consequences? And why do they care so much about what their friends think? The answer, according to neuroscientists, lies in the brain itself — specifically, in how the teenage brain develops.

The human brain is not fully mature until the mid-twenties. During adolescence, the brain undergoes massive changes. One of the most important areas is the prefrontal cortex, which controls decision-making, planning, and impulse control. In teenagers, this area is still under construction. Meanwhile, the part of the brain that processes emotions and rewards — the limbic system — is already fully active. This imbalance explains a lot about teenage behavior.

"Teenagers are not stupid," says Dr. Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, a neuroscientist at University College London. "They are capable of logical reasoning. But when they are with their peers, the reward center of their brain becomes hyperactive. The social approval of friends feels like a bigger reward than it does for adults. This is why peer pressure is so powerful during adolescence."

Studies have shown that teenagers take more risks when they are with friends than when they are alone. In one famous experiment, teenagers drove more recklessly in a video game when they believed their friends were watching — even though the friends were not actually in the room. The mere idea of being observed by peers was enough to change their behavior. Adults in the same experiment showed no difference between driving alone and driving "with friends."

This does not mean that teenagers cannot make good decisions. It means they need support. Parents and teachers who understand the science can help teenagers develop strategies. For example, teenagers can learn to pause before acting — to count to ten, walk away, or ask themselves, "What would I do if no one was watching?" Over time, these habits strengthen the prefrontal cortex and build better decision-making skills.

"The teenage brain is like a car with a powerful accelerator and weak brakes," says Dr. Blakemore. "The accelerator is the emotional, reward-seeking part of the brain. The brakes are the logical, planning part. With practice and guidance, the brakes get stronger. But during the teenage years, the car is naturally going to speed sometimes."

Writing
Use Cause and Effect to Explain a Decision You'd Make
Writing Strategy — Showing Cause and Effect:
1. State your decision clearly in the topic sentence.
2. Explain the causes — why you are making this choice. Use facts, examples, or personal reasons.
3. Explain the effects — what will happen as a result. Use conditional sentences to show possible outcomes.
4. Use transition words to connect your ideas: because, since, as a result, therefore, consequently, if...then.
5. Conclude by restating why your decision is the best one.

Model Paragraph: My Decision About Social Media

I have decided to limit my social media use to 30 minutes per day because I have noticed that excessive screen time negatively affects my mental health and academic performance. First, when I spend more than an hour scrolling through social media, I feel anxious and compare myself to others, which lowers my self-esteem. Second, since I started reducing my screen time, my grades have improved significantly because I have more time to focus on my studies. As a result of this change, I sleep better and feel more present in my daily life. If I continue this habit, then I will develop healthier relationships and achieve my academic goals. Therefore, limiting social media is the best decision for my overall well-being.

Exercise B — Write your own cause-and-effect paragraph

Choose one of these decisions and write a paragraph (120–150 words) explaining your choice using cause and effect. Include at least one conditional sentence.

Outline: State decision → Cause 1 + explanation → Cause 2 + explanation → Effect 1 (with conditional) → Effect 2 → Conclusion

Speaking
Analyze How You Handle Peer Pressure
Exercise A — Peer Pressure Scenarios

Read each scenario and decide what you would do. Then discuss with a partner.

Scenario 1: Your friends want to skip class to go to the beach. They say, "Everyone is doing it." You have an important test tomorrow. What would you do?
Scenario 2: Your group project partner suggests copying information from the internet without citing the source. They say, "No one will know." What would you do?
Scenario 3: Your friends are making fun of a new student. They expect you to laugh along. What would you do?
1. How do you usually respond to peer pressure?
2. What helps you make the right decision under pressure?
Speaking Strategy — Discussing Peer Pressure:

Describing your reaction: "When I am under pressure, I usually..." / "In that situation, I would..." / "I tend to..."
Explaining your reasoning: "The reason I would do that is..." / "I would choose that because..." / "My decision would be based on..."
Using conditionals: "If I were in that situation, I would..." / "If my friends did that, I would probably..."
Giving advice: "If I were you, I would..." / "You might want to consider..." / "One thing you could do is..."
Roleplay: The Intervention

Student A (The Friend): You are trying to convince your friend to do something risky — sneaking into a concert without tickets. Use peer pressure tactics: "Everyone is doing it," "Don't be boring," "Nothing bad will happen." Be persistent.

Student B (The Resister): You do not want to do it. Use conditional sentences to explain the consequences: "If we get caught, we will..." "If something goes wrong, my parents will..." Stay firm but polite. Offer an alternative.

Student C (The Observer): Watch the conversation. Afterward, evaluate both students' strategies. Who made the stronger argument? What could each person have done better?

The Decision Challenge
Scenario: The Scholarship Dilemma

Work in groups of three. You have been offered two scholarships. Discuss the options and make a group decision. Use conditional sentences and cause-and-effect language.

🎓 Option A: Full Scholarship to a Local University
Covers tuition and books. You can live at home. Your family is happy. But the university is not highly ranked, and the program is not your first choice.
✈️ Option B: Partial Scholarship to a Top University Abroad
Covers 60% of tuition. You must pay the rest and living expenses. You would need a part-time job and a student loan. The program is excellent, but you would be far from family and friends.
